message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the key protections and responsibilities that apply to residential tenants in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and general landlord‑tenant law. While this list is comprehensive, it’s not exhaustive—specific situations may involve additional rules or nuances. | Category | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | Common Pitfalls | |----------|------------------------|--------------------|-----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions.
• Landlord must provide a written itemized statement of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any receipts for repairs you performed.
• Request the deposit return in writing if it’s delayed. | • Landlords sometimes claim “unreasonable” deductions; you can dispute them in court. | | **Habitability** | • The property must be safe, clean, and fit for living (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical). | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If the landlord fails to fix, you may withhold rent or repair & deduct (see below). | • “Repair and deduct” is limited to certain repairs; you must follow the correct procedure. | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, **provided**:
 1. The issue is a “material defect” (e.g., broken heating, plumbing).
 2. You give the landlord **30 days’ notice**.
 3. You keep receipts and give the landlord a chance to fix it. | • Document the defect, give notice, then repair.
• Deduct the cost from the next rent payment. | • If the landlord has already repaired, you can’t deduct. | | **Rent Increases** | • For month‑to‑month leases, landlords can raise rent at the end of each lease term or with **30 days’ written notice** for month‑to‑month. | • Ask for a written notice of the increase. | • Some local ordinances (e.g., Austin, Dallas) cap rent increases for certain units. | | **Eviction** | • Landlords must provide a **written notice** (usually 3–30 days depending on reason).
• Eviction must be filed in court; the landlord cannot forcibly remove you. | • Respond to the notice in writing.
• Attend the court hearing. | • “No‑cause” evictions are allowed, but the landlord still must follow the legal process. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord may enter only for:
 1. Repairs, inspections, or showing the unit to prospective tenants/buyers.
 2. With **24‑hour written notice** (or 48 hours for emergencies). | • Keep a log of any entries. | • Landlords can’t enter without notice or a valid reason. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | • Some local ordinances add protections (e.g., LGBTQ+ status). | | **Lease Termination** | • You can terminate a lease early if the landlord breaches the lease (e.g., fails to maintain habitability).
• You may also terminate if the landlord violates your privacy or engages in unlawful conduct. | • Provide written notice of termination and document the landlord’s breach. | • Breaking a lease without cause can lead to forfeiture of the security deposit. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease. | • Pay on time; keep receipts or bank records. | • Late fees are allowed only if specified in the lease. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility bills and keep copies. | • If utilities are included, the landlord must maintain them. | | **Insurance** | • Tenants are encouraged to carry renter’s insurance. | • Obtain a policy covering personal property and liability. | • Landlord’s insurance does not cover tenant belongings. | | **Legal Remedies** | • Small claims court (up to $20,000) for disputes over deposits, unpaid rent, or damages.
• Texas courts can award damages, attorney fees, and costs. | • File a claim in the appropriate county court. | • Ensure you have documentation (photos, receipts, correspondence). | --- #### Quick Checklist for New Tenants 1. **Read the Lease Thoroughly** – Pay attention to security deposit terms, pet policies, maintenance responsibilities, and notice periods. 2. **Document the Unit** – Take photos or videos of the unit’s condition before moving in. 3. **Keep All Correspondence** – Save emails, letters, and text messages with your landlord. 4. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some cities (Austin, Dallas, Houston) have additional tenant protections (rent control, eviction moratoria, etc.). 5. **Maintain Records** – Keep receipts for any repairs you perform or rent payments. --- #### When to Seek Legal Help - **Unlawful Eviction**: If you’re being removed without proper notice or court order. - **Discrimination Claims**: If you suspect the landlord is discriminating against you. - **Large Security Deposit Disputes**: If the landlord refuses to return the deposit or gives vague deductions. - **Habitability Issues**: If the landlord repeatedly fails to fix major problems. You can consult a local attorney, a tenant‑rights organization (e.g., Texas Tenants Union), or the Texas Attorney General’s Office for guidance. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Property Code** | Statutory rights and obligations. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | File discrimination complaints. | | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection** | Guidance on landlord‑tenant disputes. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Groups** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance. | | **HUD – Fair Housing** | Federal discrimination enforcement. | --- **Bottom Line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a habitable home, timely return of your security deposit, privacy, and protection against discrimination. If your landlord violates these rights, you can pursue remedies through written notices, repair‑and‑deduct, or legal action. Always keep detailed records and know the specific statutes that apply to your city or county.
